A.explanation: Motion at right-angles has no component along the Sun-Earth line, so it gives no approaching or receding Doppler shift.

B.explanation: Whole-Sun recession would shift all the light to longer wavelength, giving only $\lambda > \lambda_s$, not a band on both sides.

C.explanation: Whole-Sun approach would shift all the light to shorter wavelength, giving only $\lambda < \lambda_s$, not a band on both sides.

D.explanation: Rotation gives one limb moving towards Earth and the opposite limb moving away, producing blue shift and red shift at the same time.

hints: Notice the observation is a band at one instant from less than $\lambda_s$ to more than $\lambda_s$, not a single shifted wavelength.
Recall Doppler shift of light depends on the component of source velocity along the line joining Sun and Earth: approach shortens $\lambda$, recession lengthens $\lambda$.
Ask which motion can give approaching, receding and near-zero line-of-sight velocities from different parts of the Sun at the same time.
walkthrough: Identify the key observation: light emitted as $\lambda_s$ is seen on Earth as a spread with some $\lambda < \lambda_s$ and some $\lambda > \lambda_s$ simultaneously.
State the Doppler rule: a source component moving towards the observer gives a blue shift to shorter wavelength, and a component moving away gives a red shift to longer wavelength.
Test whole-body motion: if the Sun as a whole moved away, every part would be receding and only $\lambda > \lambda_s$ would be seen; if towards, only $\lambda < \lambda_s$ would be seen.
Test transverse motion: motion at right-angles to the Sun-Earth line has zero velocity towards or away from Earth, so no wavelength shift is expected.

Consider rotation: one edge of the rotating Sun moves towards Earth while the opposite edge moves away, and the centre has little line-of-sight motion, so blue-shifted, red-shifted and unshifted $\lambda_s$ light arrive together and form the observed band. This is option D.
